fixes.explanation: That's the reason David gives. The psalm says, "For his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin." (Psalm 36:2) He can't detect it, and he can't hate it either. I think when you're that full of yourself, spotting your own mistakes gets awfully hard.

David doesn't mention God's law or any lessons in this verse. The reason he gives is that the man's eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin (Psalm 36:2). So the verse points to conceit. I think plenty of folks could hand him a book and he'd still be busy admiring his own reflection.

Friends never show up in this verse. David says, "…his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin." (Psalm 36:2) The reason he gives is the man's own conceit. I think he's just too full of himself to look.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, "The words of his mouth are wicked and deceitful; he has ceased to be wise and well-doing." (Psalm 36:3) Wicked and deceitful is how David describes the words of his mouth. David isn't being gentle here.
Yes, on his bed. David says, "Even on his bed he plots wickedness…" (Psalm 36:4) That's a place most of us go to rest, and he's still scheming. I think this man doesn't clock out.
The city gate isn't in this psalm. David says the man plots wickedness "Even on his bed…" (Psalm 36:4) The surprise is the bed. I think a bed is the last place you'd expect a plot.

The temple courts never come up in this psalm. David says the man plots wickedness "Even on his bed…" (Psalm 36:4) A BED! That's where most of us go to flop over and snore, and I think this man is in there cooking up a scheme instead. That's the surprising spot.
True, baker. David says, "he sets himself on a path that is not good…" (Psalm 36:4) Notice who does the setting: he sets himself on it.

Not quite, friend. David says, "he sets himself on a path that is not good; he fails to reject evil." (Psalm 36:4) So David does say it, and the man is the one doing the setting. The same verse adds that he fails to reject evil.

Not this time, baker. David says, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens, Your faithfulness to the clouds." (Psalm 36:5) That "Your" is aimed at the LORD. David is speaking right to Him.

Look again, friend. David says, "O LORD, You preserve man and beast." (Psalm 36:6) People and animals, both in the same breath, so the statement is true. And the beasts get named right alongside us, which makes me happy.
A rock isn't the picture David uses here. He says people "…take refuge in the shadow of Your wings!" (Psalm 36:7) The picture is wings, and the shadow they cast.
That's the one. David says, "For with You is the fountain of life…" (Psalm 36:9) Life itself, and it's with God. I think that's good news for everybody.
The spring of Gihon doesn't appear in this psalm. David says, "For with You is the fountain of life…" (Psalm 36:9) The fountain is with God, and he calls it the fountain of life.

Not that one, baker. David says, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You…" (Psalm 36:10) The word is know. Forgetting isn't in the verse, and his prayer is for loving devotion to reach those who know God.

Not that one, friend. The verse says, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You…" (Psalm 36:10) The word is know, and that one little word is the whole difference. I once misread a recipe card by a single word, and trust me, the cookies told on me.
A crown never comes up in this psalm. David prays, "…nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) That's what he asks God not to let happen. Losing a title isn't in the verse.

Nice guess for a psalm, but no. David prays, "…nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) What he asks is that the hand of the wicked not drive him away. His songs aren't mentioned in the verse.
